subtopic: UNITED STATES RESIGNATION OF JOHN FOSTER

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: UNITED STATES RESIGNATION OF JOHN FOSTER
subsubtopic: DULLES AS SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, members of the house will have heard the announcement this morning by the President of the United States to the effect that due to the state of health of Hon. John Foster Dulles, his resignation has been necessitated as Secretary of State of the United States of America. While I realize that this is not an occasion to give an evaluation of his services to the free world, it will be generally agreed that in the six years or more that Mr. Dulles has been in the position of secretary of state he has given direction to the foreign policy of his country with dedicated purpose, with superb courage and with unchallengeable integrity, and that his views and judgments have left their imprint on the history of these postwar years and the history of all peoples of the world who believe in freedom and its maintenance.
Canadians will honour him for the understanding and sympathy he has shown at all times in the solution of the problems which arise from time to time between our country and the United States. I believe I express the sentiments of Canadians as a whole when I say that we hope Mr. Dulles will continue to be associated in some less onerous way with the formulation of the foreign policy of the United States, particularly in view of the fact that one and probably two major conferences will take place in the months ahead, at which mankind hopes new milestones will be achieved to the peace and freedom to which Mr. Dulles gave so unstintingly of his outstanding qualities of mind and heart.

speakeroldname: Hon. L. B. Pearson (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: UNITED STATES RESIGNATION OF JOHN FOSTER
subsubtopic: DULLES AS SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in common I
think with other members of the House of Commons I learned with very great regret this morning that reasons of health had compelled the resignation of Mr. Dulles as Secretary of State of the United States. His work in building up the forces of collective resistance in free democracies against aggression has been of immense value. He never spared himself in that work, which he carried on with energy and determination which at times seemed almost superhuman and which undoubtedly was the main reason for the breakdown in his health which has now led to his resignation. If any man was ever a casualty in battle for the things in which he believed, Mr. Dulles is that man.
When I worked with him, Mr. Speaker, I did not always find myself in complete agreement with all his plans or policies, but I was always in agreement with his objectives. I deeply respected his devotion to his ideals and I admired his indomitable courage, the almost religious zeal which he displayed in pursuit of the purposes in which he believed. In Mr. Dulles' resignation the United States has lost a towering and dedicated public servant, and the cause of freedom has lost a great champion.

subtopic: UNITED STATES RESIGNATION OF JOHN FOSTER
subsubtopic: DULLES AS SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: We in the C.C.F. regret very much this further indication of the continued deterioration in the health of Mr. John Foster Dulles. Our position in regard to his policies has been made known from time to time. We think it is better at this time to make no detailed or particular comment, but merely say that history itself will judge John Foster Dulles and his policies. We recognize his strong character and the great fight he is waging against this dreadful disease. We regret very much that his health has made it impossible for him to continue the active life that has been his for so many years.

I wish to direct a question to the Minister of Justice.


Has the minister's attention been drawn to a report in last night's Ottawa Journal concerning a certain Constable Campbell of the R.C.M.P. and an alleged assault by him upon a Mr. Jones? If so, has the minister made any investigation, and would he care to make any comment thereon?

speakeroldname: Hon. E. D. Fulton (Minister of Justice):
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: ALLEGED ASSAULT UPON CIVILIAN BY MEMBER OF FORCE
speechtext:
Yes, I have seen the press report, and I have obtained preliminary reports from the officers of the R.C.M.P. I am advised that as soon as oral word was received on Saturday night from the solicitor acting for Mr. Jones, alleging this assault, the R.C.M.P. authorities made an investigation. This inquiry resulted in a vigorous and complete denial by Constable Campbell-and this was confirmed by the two other policemen who were with him -that he had in any way assaulted Mr. Jones.
Following the publication in yesterday's newspaper of a repetition of the accusation, the police had planned to make a further inquiry, which, on this occasion, was to take the form of an inquiry under oath. Before this could be commenced, however, word was received that Constable Campbell has himself started a civil action for libel against, I believe, both the newspaper and the solicitor who, I understand, made the allegation. After we received word that a civil action had been started we, of course, deferred the further inquiry under oath. That inquiry will be deferred pending the outcome of the civil litigation.

speechtext:
Yes. I am informed that a lengthy meeting took place yesterday afternoon between Mr. Donald Gordon, president of the Canadian National Railways, with other senior officials of the railway, and Mr. W. E. Gamble, vice president of the brotherhood of locomotive firemen and enginemen, accompanied by the general chairman of the union. After detailed discussion the union representatives refused to consider an agreement which would implement the recommendations of the recent federal conciliation board concerning wages and working conditions of the C.N.R. firemen.
Prior to this and other meetings the railway company had relinquished its claim for

complete managerial discretion in the employment of firemen helpers and had accepted the recommendations of the board of conciliation, which were based on the principles of the Kellock commission report. In these circumstances the company has therefore informed the union representatives that it has no responsible alternative but to implement the recommendations of the board of conciliation, and a notice is being prepared outlining the amendments to existing conditions of service to take effect as from May 1, 1959.
This notice will be delivered to the union representatives today over the signature of Mr. S. F. Dingle, vice president, operations, and concurrently a personal letter is being sent, over the signature of the president, to all C.N.R. firemen and hostlers enclosing a copy of the notice and explaining its effect.
I am further informed that Mr. Gamble has announced that authorization to strike has been given by the membership of two regions, and that strike authorization is being sought in the third. Management has made it clear to the union that they intend to operate the railway even if this membership withdraws from service.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I should like to direct a question to the Minister of Trade and Commerce arising out of a serious situation in northeastern Saskatchewan, where large quantities of tough and damp grain on farms are in danger of spoiling. Will the minister consider asking the wheat board to institute additional emergency quotas for tough and damp grain only, particularly in view of the unanimous resolution of the Saskatchewan legislature requesting that this be done?

speakeroldname: Hon. Gordon Churchill (Minister of Trade and Commerce):
subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR MOVEMENT OF TOUGH AND DAMP GRAIN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this question was raised on March 3 by the hon. member for Mackenzie (Mr. Korchinski), who has a greater interest in this problem than even the hon. member for Assiniboia. It was also drawn to my attention by the hon. member for Humboldt-Melfort (Mr. Rapp). Neither of those gentlemen depended upon a resolution passed by the provincial legislature of Saskatchewan in order to draw attention to this serious problem.
Now that the hon. member for Assiniboia is aware of the problem I do not mind repeating and enlarging on the answer I gave on March 3, if it is in accordance with the rules of the house. The problem at this time is not so much one of higher quotas but rather one of sufficient storage facilities at terminal positions to accommodate the volume of grain which must be moved.
The board has been making every effort during the winter months to move high moisture grain out of country positions as rapidly as possible, and for several weeks shipments to the lakehead have been confined largely to this type of grain. As a result quotas in the northeastern area of Saskatchewan are at a generally higher level than in other parts of the west. However, storage facilities at the lakehead have been congested for a considerable period of time, and

no large volume of grain can be moved to this destination until after the opening of navigation.
I am assured by the board that immediately space becomes available with the opening of navigation, priority in shipments will continue to be given to high moisture grain, and the railways and handling companies have been so instructed. The railways, in anticipation of the opening of navigation, have already commenced to load grain in volume for the lakehead, and as a result a heavier movement of this out of condition grain is already under way.
Within a very short period of time I am confident that producers in the northeastern area of Saskatchewan with high moisture grain will be provided with additional delivery opportunity in an effort to alleviate the danger of such grain going out of condition.

Mr. Speaker, in rising to speak today on the budget I am sure that all those who listened to the news broadcast at eight o'clock this morning would think me remiss if I did not offer my congratulations to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) on having been selected by the press as the next secretary of state for external affairs. I may say that I join with the press in this tribute to the urbanity of the hon. gentleman and to the tact and diplomacy with which he has always conducted himself in the house.
I may say I do so with even more satisfaction because the post, for reasons which we all so much regret, had scarcely become vacant before I suggested to my colleagues that the most likely successor was the Minister of Finance. I am sure the Prime Minister knowing that was my judgment, will not hesitate to make my prediction come true, though I knew a prime minister in the past who took a certain satisfaction in disappointing the press and even at times, in disappointing the opposition.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Do you remember one who disappointed you very recently?

maintopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
No, I know of no prime minister, except one, who has disappointed me recently and that is the right hon. gentleman who sits opposite. I was only one of about a million people who have a close interest in the province of Newfoundland who were disappointed by his announcement.
Now, sir, a budget is after all only a reflection of housekeeping. It is a reflection of good housekeeping, or of bad. It does seem to me that the test of a budget is perhaps not so much in what that budget contains, about which I feel there are many of my colleagues on this side of the house more competent to speak than I am-

maintopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear.

maintopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
-such as the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River (Mr. Benidickson) and the hon. member for Welland (Mr. McMillan), to mention only two who have

The Budget-Mr. Pickersgill already dealt very effectively with the presentation made by the minister the other evening.
I intend to speak on the general theme of good faith and good management, which seem to me to be the two tests that should be applied and which in fact are applied in the long run and sometimes in a quite short run to any government. I want to recall to the minds of hon. members, particularly to hon. members in the Conservative party to my left who perhaps were not here at the time, a few words that were uttered in this house from a seat very close to the one I now occupy, by Right Hon. Louis St. Laurent on the only occasion when he spoke on the address in reply to the speech from the throne as leader of the opposition. His remarks will be found at page 43 of Hansard for October 16, 1957. Mr. St. Laurent said:
It is over 22 years since the Liberal party was last in opposition. In the 22 years Canada has enjoyed-I use a word that I believe will become more widely used in that connection as time passes -I say in the 22 years that Canada has enjoyed a Liberal government we as Liberals have prided ourselves on the fact that every item on the program placed before the public in each successive campaign has been implemented in full whenever it was possible for the government or for the parliament of Canada acting alone to implement it.
He went on to say:
This is a record of which we are justly proud. We are also proud of the fact that in these past 20 years the people of Canada have come to take it for granted that the government of Canada acts in good faith and carries out its undertakings to the people. I believe that the good faith in fulfilling undertakings that the public has received from the Liberal government they will now expect to receive from a Conservative government.
I propose to examine a few highlights because, with the record of this government, I will only have time for that, and apply to them the test that Mr. St. Laurent suggested at the very opening of the first parliament after this government took office. I also want, before doing that, to draw to the attention of the house something else Mr. St. Laurent said in that speech at page 45 of Hansard, because it seems to me it is very relevant to what we are considering here now. He said:
We are all looking forward to the presentation of this budget-
That was in the last parliament.
-and to a full debate on the case the Minister of Finance will present at that time.
Then I would ask hon. members, particularly those who were here at the time, to mark these words:
From time to time I have noticed from press rumours that the government intends to make important changes in the fiscal policy of this country without giving the elected representatives of the Canadian people an opportunity for a full debate

which, under our parliamentary system, is afforded by the presentation of a budget.
This is Mr. St. Laurent speaking.
I refuse to believe that a government whose leading members made so much of their attachment to the rights of parliament would seriously propose, both to alter the tax structure of the country and to increase expenditures substantially without giving parliament every opportunity afforded by the rules to consider the whole financial picture and to debate fully the benefits of proposed changes upon the economy.
But that, sir, is precisely what this government did. It is true that the Minister of Finance told us before that parliament met that he was going to bring down a budget. But then he got a message from "le grand chef", who had gone to London, telling him he had made a mistake. "Le grand chef" was not presenting a budget, so there was no budget. The result, of course, gave "le grand chef" an opportunity which he would not otherwise have had; because if we had had a budget in December, 1957 the Prime Minister would not have been able to come into this house with that document which, in the most dishonest performance I have ever seen in this house, on January 20-

maintopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Shame, shame.

maintopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE

maintopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I hope the hon. member will reconsider the adjective he used.

speechtext: And withdraw it.

maintopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I am not going to waste my time by considerations of that sort. I will say the most incredible performance I have ever seen in this house.

maintopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker-

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, on a point of order-

maintopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: As I was saying when I was so rudely interrupted by the new secretary of state for external affairs-

maintopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The Prime Minister, on that occasion that we all remember, read bits and pieces out of their context from a document which was not intended for publication and which was refuted in a most complete way by the Minister of Finance

himself on June 17 last in his previous budget speech, as one of my colleagues will show later in this debate. We had the same old straw threshed over again and the same old tiresome story by the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Nowlan) the other night. He said the Minister of Finance might not have brought down such a budget as he did if they had only known the truth, if Mr. Harris had not concealed it.
Now, sir, when the Prime Minister spoke on January 20, 1958 this government had been in office for seven months, and they stand convicted out of the mouth of the Minister of National Revenue of being so stupid, so incompetent that in seven months they could not find out for themselves what they claim Mr. Harris knew and hid three months before that. This is what the Prime Minister asked the people to believe. With that capacity for making black seem white, which no doubt convinced many juries in the past, he perhaps convinced his last jury; because I do not think he will ever convince another.

maintopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Neither will you.

maintopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: We will see about that. I certainly do not hesitate to appear before the jury that passes on me. If the Prime Minister would like to come and contest my seat with me, it would not give me a bit of worry.

maintopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Oh, oh.

maintopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I want to deal first of all with the most recent example we have had of bad management and bad faith, both at once, by the present government. I refer to the recent amendment to the immigration regulations. Now, sir, as a prelude to what I have to say I want to admit that no sensible person would urge the government at this time, when they have the economy in such a deplorable state, when there is such a level of unemployment, to open wide the floodgates of immigration. No one is suggesting that. But we did have an unnecessary and cruel act performed the other day.
I should like to draw attention to what was said about that act by the Prime Minister on April 7 last in answer to a question by the hon. member for Davenport (Mr. Morton). He suggested that if there was any discrimination in that order, that discrimination was not in the order itself but was in an order in council that was passed on May 24, 1956.
Now, sir, there is always discrimination in the selection of immigrants. Everyone knows there are only two ways to avoid discrimination. One is to let everybody in and the other is to let nobody in. What we want to avoid is improper, unfair and cruel discrimination. I am not suggesting it was the discriminatory
The Budget

Mr. Pickersgill character, but it was the restrictive character of this recent order that was at fault. What is really more extraordinary, sir, is that here was a law-because this order in council is part of the law of Canada until it is changed -enacted by the governor in council on March 19, though it was not published for quite some time after that, and here is what the Prime Minister said about it on April 7, as recorded at page 2296 of Hansard:
I, for one, intend to have this looked into-
He says on April 7 he intends to have it looked into.
-because the section indicates that the one passed in 1956 had whatever objections can be raised against the present amendment.
Any of us who served under Mr. St. Laurent when he was prime minister know that he would not have had to come to the house two weeks later and admit that he had not taken the trouble to read a document that was before the cabinet and that was to be made a law affecting the lives of people. That was not the way he presided over the government of this country, and it seems to me that no more shocking example of the mismanagement of the Prime Minister could be found than that which the Prime Minister himself gave by that statement.
We are told by the Department of Citizenship and Immigration, or by some so-called spokesman for that department, that the reason they made this unnecessary, cruel and inhuman order was to give preference to skilled workers. Of course that is the most unadulterated camouflage; there is not the slightest intention on the part of the government of doing anything about that at all. This order was just a restriction. It was an unnecessary and inhuman restriction, and it was aimed at one community in this country; it was aimed at those people of Italian origin.

maintopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Nonsense.

maintopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: The reason it was done, sir, was that when the government realized that more people of Italian origin than people from the United Kingdom came in last year, they got in a panic. They were afraid of many of their political supporters, and they felt they had to do something about it. Then they did this stupid, cruel, silly and inhuman thing.

maintopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: That is pure nonsense.

maintopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman can make his speech on his own time and it will, no doubt, be pure nonsense.
By restricting the number and relationship of the persons who can be sponsored the government has worked the greatest hardship upon many other communities, particularly
2712	HOUSE OF
The Budget-Mr. Pickersgill those people from Poland who for the first time in many years are in some small numbers able to get out of their country, and who, at a time when they can get out, are being met with a slam of the door by this country.
What is more, Mr. Speaker, this was a grave affront to parliament. This order was passed on March 19. We were considering the estimates up until March 18. I happen to know something about the way in which cabinets are run. I know perfectly well that an order in council is not passed on March 19 unless a recommendation has been in the privy council office some days previously. In other words, the government knew perfectly well and the minister knew perfectly well that this recommendation was before parliament at the time when we were considering the estimates. Every member who spoke on both sides of the house complained that the minister was too tough and too restrictive in her treatment of sponsored immigrants. Not a word did she breathe about this restrictive order that she intended to have passed the very day we were denied, under the rules, the opportunity to debate it in the normal course. Then the moment parliament disposed of the estimates the order was passed and, as the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) admitted, without any consideration.
Also, when I suggested that this was a rather dubious procedure, the Prime Minister took it upon himself to say, as reported at page 2296 of Hansard:
-I am not sure that the hon. gentleman is strictly right in the lecture on procedure inherent in his question, because I seem to recollect that a similar situation arose when he was minister.
Even if that had been true, it is no excuse for the conduct of the government. If I did something wrong, that is not the slightest excuse for their doing something wrong. But that happens to be totally, completely and utterly untrue in every syllable. Every amendment which I proposed and which the governor in council made to the regulations was announced well before the estimates or during the estimates. One or two procedural changes which were not amendments to the law I announced in the house or in the estimates committee, as the hon. member for Kamloops (Mr. Fulton) will recall, while we were actually carrying on our proceedings, because in one case he took the most violent exception to what was suggested. Hence, whatever else may be said about any of these things, no one can say that I ever at any time attempted to make regulations or


to get the governor in council to make regulations at a time when there was not full opportunity given to parliament to deal with them.
There is no need for a long speech on the budget by the hon. lady in order to deal with this matter. All she needs to do is to come in here honestly and admit her mistake, say that this stupid and inhuman order has been revoked and that they have gone back to the situation which subsisted for four years and which for two years the government has had a chance to change, if there was anything wrong with it; and which they did nothing about. I would strongly suggest to the hon. lady, if she were here, that instead of getting the Tory machine to write her one of those essays to say "The Liberals did this and the Liberals did that", she just come in and deal with what she herself was responsible for, say it was a mistake, make the change and get on with the business of the house.
I can deal only briefly with each of these points, but I come now to what I regard as the most shocking example of bad management we have had from the present government. I refer, of course, to the handling of the Arrow.

maintopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Oh, oh.

maintopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Your ammunition is all wet.

maintopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hon. gentleman will not expect me to pose as a military expert, and I am not going to do so.

maintopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Or any other kind.

maintopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Or any other kind, someone says. No, I am simply a representative of the people here in parliament representing some of the taxpayers of this country.
The Prime Minister came in here and told us on February 20, as reported at page 1222 of Hansard, as follows:
-frankness demands that I advise that at present there Is no other work that the government can assign immediately to the companies that have been working on the Arrow and its engine . . . We must not abdicate our responsibility to assure that the huge sums which it is our duty to ask parliament to provide for defence are being expended in the most effective way to achieve that purpose.
Everyone would agree with that second statement. But if that was the case, Mr. Speaker, surely one of two things should have happened after that announcement by the Prime Minister in September. Surely the Prime Minister and the government should have given their attention to putting something in place of the Arrow. There was no possible shadow of excuse for carrying on this program one day after September when the

Prime Minister now says he reached the conclusion that this machine was obsolete, except the determination to find something else to put in its place. The government did absolutely nothing about trying to find anything else to put in its place. Instead of that, the Prime Minister made this statement which is like the Delphic oracle which was interpreted in two different ways according to the desires of the people who interpreted it. Then he went off on a trip around the world.
I am going to suggest what would have happened if Mr. St. Laurent or Mr. C. D. Howe had had to deal with this problem. In the first place, I suggest that no speech would have been made in September at all. When they realized, if they had, that this was no longer a proper military program and that we had to have the kind of co-operation with the United States about which the Prime Minister talked so much, I suggest that instead of going thousands and thousands of miles in another direction they would have gone to Washington and they would have stayed in Washington until they got results, just as Mr. St. Laurent did with regard to the St. Lawrence seaway within three months of becoming prime minister. The St. Lawrence seaway would not have been built today if Mr. St. Laurent had not gone to Washington on February 7, 1949 and had that conference with Mr. Truman which my friend the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson) will recall.
The other thing, of course, that was absolutely incredible about the management of the Arrow was this statement which the Prime Minister made about the dismissal of the employees, and I think I should read it. It is to be found at page 1306 of Hansard of February 23. He said:
Was there any justification to say to everybody, "You are out", and today announce, if the press is correct, that some 2,500 are called hack? What was the reason for that precipitate action? Was it necessary? In the estimates it was shown that a further amount of some $50 million, was to be expended . . . Why rush them out on Friday afternoon if it was not for some purpose other than the benefit of those employees?
Some days later after that insinuation had gone all over the country and could never be caught up with the government produced the telegrams that were sent from the Department of Defence Production ordering the company to stop work immediately and dispose of its employees. That is why the company had to do it. I am sure they did not do it out of any choice. They did it because they were ordered to do it by the government and because they could not have received another cent out of the contract, as the hon. member for Laurier (Mr. Chevrier) demonstrated in the house, in order to pay
The Budget-Mr. Pickersgill wages. It is true they could pay severance pay but severance pay is not wages.
The hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River (Mr. Benidickson) and I have searched carefully through the estimates and we cannot And that elusive $50 million. Of course, $50 million is apparently a very small sum for this government, but for the taxpayers it is still a large sum of money. The casual way in which the Prime Minister was tossing about $50 million was, I suggest, characteristic of this whole business. It seems to me there was one of two things that could have been done last September about this matter. I may say that I am merely talking about mismanagement and about the budget and about financial responsibilities. One was to stop the production then if the government were not going to do anything whatever about it, as in the event happened-they did nothing -and save that money for the taxpayers. The other was-and I think it would have been a far better course-for the Prime Minister and the Minister of Defence Production (Mr. O'Hurley) and anyone else who might have any influence in Washington, to go to Washington and try to do something about it. But that is not the kind of management of the affairs of this country that we get nowadays.
The other thing about the Arrow which was a very great shock to us was this. Nobody could understand for a long time why February 20 was chosen by the Prime Minister as the date to cancel the contract. Then on March 3 the Prime Minister's supporter and friend, the hon. member for Rosedale (Mr. Walker), got up and told us why suddenly on February 20, without any warning of any kind or preparation of the employees of any sort, this order was issued. This statement was made in the house. Here are the words of the hon. member for Rosedale. He said, as reported on page 1566 of Hansard for March 3 last:
-a high priced film which was intended to show, subtly, that the Arrow was going strong. Ostensibly the film was supposed to mark the 50th anniversary of flight in Canada but it was mostly about the Arrow. It was offered free to TV stations across the land-

speechtext: That is not a point of order.

speechtext: Order. If the hon. member has a point of order I will hear him.

maintopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Then we had a lot of real or synthetic indignation about lobbies and how a government which really had the interests of the public at heart would resist all lobbies. I will quote the Prime Minister on the subject of lobbies when he was not Prime Minister, in another session, so I do not think the Prime Minister can prevent these words from going on Hansard. On July 24, 1956 the Prime Minister was speaking on the tax-sharing arrangements in the debate on Mr. Harris' bill, and this is what he said as reported on page 6368:
I do not want to involve myself in any maritime argument-
He has changed from that too since then!
-but I would say this. There is one difference between the members from the maritimes and those from the western provinces, and it is this. While we from the western provinces do disagree, sometimes on the basis of partisanship, none the less when the welfare of the western provinces is being discussed and in particular when our major subject, agricultural production, is being discussed, we bury our disagreements and unite for the common benefit of the western provinces. Sometimes, as I listened to my hon. friends from the maritimes upholding those things which they themselves assuredly cannot support other than vocally, 1 wonder whether a similar united front analogous to that being formed today by the premiers of the maritime provinces would not have a most beneficial effect upon the economy of the maritimes, especially if that analogy were continued and extended into the House of Commons.
In other words, what the Prime Minister advocated when he was over on this side was that we should have regional lobbies right here in the house itself. Now he objects to other Canadians elsewhere seeking by legitimate means to protect their interests.

maintopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Oh, oh.

maintopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
We can see, of course, how terrified the followers of the hon. gentleman are, because when we on this side of the house have attempted to describe the coal crisis in Nova Scotia and seek to get something done about it we have seen how frightened the hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Maclnnis) was-I am sorry he is not here now-to have it discussed. He was so


afraid that somebody might say something which might hurt the feelings of the Prime Minister and might indispose him to the Nova Scotian coal miners, with the result that nothing would be done about it. It seems to me, Mr. Speaker, that we have reached the stage where if you open your mouth and say something on behalf of your constituents it is a lobby, and nothing can be done about the problem; if you keep quiet and say nothing, then there is no problem and nothing needs to be done. Well, that is a wonderful way of carrying on government!
I would have liked to have had the time to deal with those Atlantic resolutions of the Conservative party about which so much was made before the 1957 election. We all remember that great advertisement which appeared with the pictures of all the candidates, and all those points that they were going to bring about, but I forbear to deal with that for this reason. The other day the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) in a burst of cynicism, which was unusual for him, said as reported on page 1838, column 1, of Hansard for March 11:
That is two elections ago.
I repeat. He said:
That is two elections ago.
In other words, with regard to anything promised before 1957, there has been another election since, so it does not count. That was the attitude and the position taken by the Minister of Finance the other day in the debate to which I referred.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Are you taking into account the change in circumstances over the years?

maintopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: There was no change in circumstances. The promise the hon. gentleman was dealing with at that time was the promise to call a federal-provincial conference, and I know of no change in circumstances-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: You know of no change?

maintopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
-except the inconvenience and uncomfortable character of such a meeting for the government.
I have many other things which I had planned to say but I have perhaps been more exuberant than I would have wished and I notice my time is running out. I would like very much to go over many of these other promises made two elections ago about which nothing apparently is going to be done. I do say that no more cynical observation was ever made than that made the other day by the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Nowlan) in attempting to put a face upon this volte-face

in this budget, and a pretty poor face it was. But I do say that confidence is a plant of slow growth. It is a structure which can be built up only very slowly. Unhappily, confidence is always fragile. It is a most fragile thing, particularly in public life. I am glad that I could stand on this side of the house behind Mr. St. Laurent when he made that proud boast with which I opened my remarks. But this government will not be able to do it. Indeed, the confidence in this government is such that the only thing I can think of with which to compare it is Humpty-Dumpty. You remember that Humpty-Dumpty sat on a wall, and Humpty-Dumpty had a great fall; and I do not think that all MeKim's horses and all McKim's men will ever put the Humpty-Dumpty of confidence in this government together again.
In a provincial election in the province where I spent 30 years of my life the premier of that province is giving promises to the people that the Prime Minister has given him the assurance that the proposed $80 million Manitoba flood control scheme will be supported financially by the federal government.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: How does it look out there?

maintopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
It has looked very different since the budget from the feelings they had before the budget. Out there you have an exact duplication of the situation we had here. You have a spending spree of incredible proportions. But they have seen the morning after, here, and surely that will have some effect. But what I want to say is this: I do not think, after the record of broken promises that we have had from this government, anybody in Manitoba, even a Tory, is going to believe that there will be any contribution to Manitoba. Maybe if it was Saskatchewan it might be different. They cannot feel any confidence that there will be any contribution for them under this scheme unless an act of parliament is passed, and I do not mean just printed in the budget papers; I mean passed by parliament.
But the ultimate in bad faith is what we have seen in recent days. We have seen the Prime Minister take it upon himself to alter or seek to alter the terms of the agreement upon which two nations were joined together into one nation, and there will be other opportunities to debate this question. It will never be forgotten. I said to the Prime Minister just after he made his announcement on March 25 that every Newfoundlander would regard this as a betrayal, and he suggested that I could not speak for the Newfoundlanders. Well, I have been in Newfoundland, and I am speaking for the
The Budget-Mr. Rowe Newfoundlanders, all of them but one. And then there is the extraordinary attitude taken by the Prime Minister about the supreme court. Here is a court which for three months has been unable to function properly because it has only two judges, and the Prime Minister has the impertinence-and I use the word in its proper sense-to obtrude himself into provincial affairs and say that he will not make an appointment to that court until-

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I never said that.

maintopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: The hon. gentleman was quoted in the press as having said it. If the Prime Minister wants to deny it he can do so afterwards, but not in my time. The hon. gentleman was quoted as having said that he would not appoint a third judge until the province had provided for a fourth.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: That is incorrect.

maintopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Imagine what would have happened if the Prime Minister had said that to Quebec or to Ontario. It is just because this is a small province. Why does he not say that to Prince Edward Island? They have three judges. They have never had more than three. We have had three judges in Newfoundland-

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: We?

maintopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Well, Newfoundland is a part of Canada, and I think I can say "we" when referring to Newfoundland, even if the Prime Minister cannot.
I can tell the Prime Minister that there is one other question about which not only the people of Newfoundland but the people of all Canada are concerned. When the Prime Minister came into this house on that black Monday and took the side of the law breakers against those who were maintaining law and order he did more to destroy confidence in his government than by any other act he has done or is likely to do, and it seems to me that of all the acts of bad faith which will be remembered against this government that will, for all time, be the worst.

maintopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as I listened to the presentation of the budget now before parliament by the Minister of Finance, I could not help but think that no one in the house within sound of his voice could help but realize his outstanding ability and his untiring industry and devotion to any task with which he has ever been confronted. I have always enjoyed listening to the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate (Mr. Pickersgill): He and I have been friends here for a long time.

The Budget-Mr. Rowe
We are proud in the rest of Canada to have Newfoundland join in confederation. It has great possibilities. It is the youngest province, but recently it has not been conspicuous for a child-like silence, and I know the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate (Mr. Pick-ersgill) must have realized that during these last several weeks. It has certainly caused some concern on the part of the government, but that concern was far exceeded by the distress and the excitement that it caused among that old and at one time happy family of Liberals across Canada. I am sure there must have been times when former cabinet members who now sit to your left, Mr. Speaker, must feel the tattered remnants of a once great party-have a gigantic task ahead of them.
I am afraid the hon. member who has just resumed his seat cannot be better described than by the words used of Lord Ronald when he said nothing, he flung himself from the room, flung himself upon his horse and rode madly off in all directions. I think that those who listen to his speech will have realized that he is still riding fast and furious, and still in all directions. I was listening carefully in case there might be something he had to say that I could follow, but I feel it would be unnecessary for me to try, along with him, to resurrect and fight two elections all over again in such rapid succession after such a serious defeat for his party.
The budget now before parliament is a difficult budget. I have listened to a great many budgets in this house. Canada is only 92 years of age. We are a young country. We have a tremendous structure, a tremendous setup of transportation facilities, and high costs to meet, but in the 92 years of our existence we have reason to have pride though it may be mingled with a certain degree of concern about high taxes, deficits and so forth. There is no reason for despair. I have seen great changes here. As a matter of fact, I have listened to substantially more than one-third of all the budgets presented since Canada was born.

maintopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: And most of the good ones.

maintopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Yes, but I have listened to just about as many from one party as from the other and I am amazed at the way Canada has survived the absence of the policies that your party did not have. Again I emphasize that this is a young country. If I may be ultra-personal, I might say that my mother and father both lived longer than Canada is old. So there is still hope yet for the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate and his leader.


The Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) was faced with a difficult problem. He had a heritage left on his doorstep because of the smug complacency of a government which was too big and which had been too long in power and which was sitting on the side lines, like Micawber, waiting for something to turn up. They told the people of Canada that there was great prosperity before them. It was a prosperity that was born of defence production; a prosperity into which they had poured $15 billion of the taxpayers' money in 15 years.
The opposition talk about the A. V. Roe situation, or any other situation in which they made such reckless and extravagant expenditures. It is true that it was perhaps difficult for them to understand matters of this kind. They were trying to keep pace with the demands which were being made during the hot war, the post war and the cold war. Had it not been for the hot war, the postwar period and the cold war period, this country, under the lack of policy of the former government, might well have lost its economic independence entirely. More than anything else it was the $15 billion that the taxpayers of Canada poured into our economy of that day that averted that situation. As I listened to the hon. member today and those who are quibbling about dollars and cents and as to whether there are 500,000 unemployed, 499,000 or 507,000, or whether it is so many millions of dollars or not, I ask this question. Do hon. members mean to tell me that this has all developed because the public changed the guard, because the public were tired of a government that had no policy and put in a new government? If you let a country drift for two or three decades, at least over two decades, you cannot repair the destruction in two years.
The party that sits to your left now, or the remnants of that one-time great party-it looks smaller to me than ever before-was very complacent. I have sat in opposition and watched them when they were so large that they did not know what to do with themselves, when they were so complacent that they left everything as it was.
I have great admiration for the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate. I have known him for many years. He was trained in political technique. I am not so sure, in fact, whether he was trained by the late Right Hon. Mackenzie King or whether he trained the late Right Hon. Mackenzie King, but at any rate between them they kept the public more or less fooled for a long time. I certainly have great regard for the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson). I have known him also for many years. The older I grow the more mellow I become. The more

experience I have the more tolerant I am of the other fellow's problems, and I see his. I do not envy him, but I do suggest to him- since he is not in the house I hope the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate will tell him-that I have nothing but the warmest regard for him, and while I cannot from over here do much to help him I would like to ask him to take a suggestion.
I suggest that the crafty attitude adopted by the late Right Hon. Mackenzie King would be an excellent one for him to follow, namely that when things look the darkest, no matter what the problem or no matter how difficult it may be, just wait and see, something will turn up. That has been more or less the policy of the Liberal party down through the years. We have seen a trend, Mr. Speaker- I am not exaggerating when I say this-over the last two decades, as I have said, in this country that had it not been for the $15 billion that was poured into defence expenditures this country might well have ended up, as far as economic dependence is concerned, as a satellite of the United States of America.
I remember how those who are now in the opposition used to come back from Washington and tell us what they told those fellows in Washington. They would say, "We told them that if they put tariffs against this or that what it would mean to us". Oh, how vigorous and loud were they. They were so loud they almost ripped the heather of the bloom in order to emphasize what they were doing. They were doing nothing more than emphasizing their own smug complacency, criticizing the other country's policy when they had none of their own.
The people of the United States are proud; they are great business gentlemen. It has been my experience in years past to do a great deal of business with leading citizens of the United States of America. I was once responsible for a company which did many millions of dollars worth of business over a period of 16 to 18 years. There are no finer business gentlemen in the world. They appreciate you far more if you run your own business and do not tell them how to run theirs. They are shrewd operators and they have much more respect for you if you shrewdly operate your own interests. They have their own economic survival to look after; they have done a good job at it and they do not object to you looking after yours.
No, Mr. Speaker, we had a government in power for many years, as you know very well-that was before you divorced yourself from politics-that always said, "We must not do anything that will be considered provocative by the United States of America".
The Budget-Mr. Rowe Oh, how those words must ring in the ears of the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate, because I do not know whether he wrote them or whether Mackenzie King wrote them. Oh, no, we must not do anything to provoke them. Down through the years that has been their attitude.
I say this for the benefit of those younger members. I know some of those older men over there who have been around nearly as long as I have been. Some of them have been around longer, by the look of their faces, I know those men. I am sure they would appreciate the fact that there has been a change of the guard and that we have a new government. They appreciate the fact that we have the most dynamic leadership in the person of the present Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) that we have had in this country for years. They must appreciate that. If they have not met some of our younger members I will introduce them to them. We have right here in this parliament a great number of young men with the greatest amount of latent ability and background of education and experience for their age that has ever sat in any party in this house since confederation. There is a great future for many of these younger men.
The present Minister of Finance, it is true, had to raise taxes. He had the unemployment problem. I ask you, Mr. Speaker, or any hon. member on the other side of the house, whether that was merely because there was a change in government in the last year or two? It was caused more by the lack of appreciation of our problems in this country by the previous government. We have problems which are purely Canadian. Our forefathers thought of them many years ago. The first leader of our party thought of them. He knew this country was large; he knew we had few people. He knew we were to have transportation carrying charges which would be higher than those that any similar number of people had. He knew we had a frigid and cold climate. He knew that we would have to protect agricultural interests and that we would have to protect industry in this country in order to provide employment for our people.
Those who are sitting to your left, Mr. Speaker, in those days were saying the same thing as an hon. member in another place said not long ago. He is one of the leaders of the Liberal party in another place. He said a few weeks ago that the only hope for Canada was the wholesale development of our own resources. May I say to the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate through you, Mr. Speaker, that had that policy been followed and if that policy is followed in the future they will not be criticizing the

The Budget-Mr. Rowe immigration department; there will be no immigration department. What we will have will be an emigration department because under that kind of government more university graduates and scholars will be trying to find jobs in the United States than will stay in Canada.
These are things that distinguish this party from this old, torn, worn, dusty group which is now almost extinct. We must look to the future, Mr. Speaker; we must plan for the future.
My hon. friend talks about high taxes. He criticized this government for high expenditures. He seems to forget the fact that the former government continued a tight money policy, but at the same time they were taking $600 to $700 million more than they needed. Out of the other side of their mouths they were criticizing Canadians for not investing enough money in our development. At the same time they took $600 to $700 million a year more than they needed and they wondered why we had no money to invest in the development of this country. Had we followed that trend, where would we have been?
I remember many of those finance ministers. I remember the Robbs, the Ilsleys, the Dunnings, the Abbotts and how each of them would change their policy from time to time as often as they changed ministers. I remember how each of them would say, "Why, this is cyclical budgeting. We are going to take the money from you now because we think we can spend it and take care of it better than you can." I remember them criticizing Canadians for not investing in our great resources like the Americans do. Would there be another depression? No, they said, we would never have a depression like we had in the 30's, a depression for which many on the other side blamed the Conservative party as being responsible even though the depression prevailed throughout the whole world.
Mr. Speaker, after taking $700 million a year more than they needed they now turn around and criticize the Minister of Finance because he found the gross national product at the highest level in the history of our country and still 10 per cent of our people are unemployed. Does not that spell a warning to everyone in the house? I say that nobody realizes more than the able Minister of Finance and the colourful and distinguished Prime Minister that there must be something wrong when you have a gross national product of that magnitude and 500,000 people unemployed.
The former government sat there smugly and complacently and disregarded the greatest

market we had. They were flying all over the world to find markets in the lowest cost countries in the world and neglecting with reckless disregard and abandon the best market the farmers have had right here in Canada, the home market.
I have had experience in several enterprises connected with raw resources, especially farming. Believe it or not, I am still a farmer. My friend from Twillingate laughs. I will take him up to my farm some day. But, Mr. Speaker, every hon. member within the sound of my voice from Quebec, Ontario or western Canada knows that it only takes about half as many people today to produce the same amount of agricultural products as it did when I entered the house first. From being connected with it I know that with modern machinery it takes only half as many people today to produce as it did a quarter of a century ago. The hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate nods approval because he knows that problem.
Where then is this country going to find employment for the increased population, a population increasing by per cent each year through new births and per cent through immigration? Where is the employment going to come from? Years ago you had to be a farmer to get into Canada but today it is a reason for being kept out of Canada because we do not need farmers. You do not need people in forestry. I remember sending a man to Europe 15 years ago to get 300 men. The hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate remembers that well because he was the minister of immigration at the time and assisted in bringing them in to work in the bush. Today half as many men will do the job.
Mr. Speaker, then we have the situation with respect to manufactured products. In that regard keep in mind the general advancement we have had in science, technology and automation. Think of the utensils that are used in the kitchen now. Our grandmothers used to wash their clothes on a washboard. Our grandfathers used to grind corn by hand for feed for the cattle. Now you press an electric button. One man today can look after as many cattle, whether dairy or beef, as 10 men did 30 years ago.
So we have all these new things coming into use. As old as some of you may think I am, I am not one of those who believe for a moment that the new machinery is going to ruin employment for the people. There will be more employment available than we have people to take advantage of it if we have a vigorous policy, if we follow the

government's policy and develop our raw resources and process more of our own requirements at home in the future, which has been the distinctive policy of the Conservative party since confederation.
The Liberal party has neglected that phase of our development. They have supported a lopsided development in this country down through the years. The result is that they hoodwinked themselves by believing that defence production would ensure permanent prosperity, and they hoodwinked the whole of Canada unconsciously. I know they would not do it seriously. These apostles of world trade have been suggesting for a quarter of a century that you have got to buy before you sell. I do not know of any business I have been connected with where that ever worked out. It has never worked out. They say that you have got to buy before you sell. What has been the result? From early days we have been buying before selling. No other country in the world buys so much per capita as Canada. We buy $273 per capita, the United States of America buys $26 to $28 per capita and Britain buys $48 per capita. We think we can buy ourselves into prosperity. We think we can buy from everybody so we can sell to somebody.
Business is not one-sided. May I say again that I have great respect for the United States government and I do not want to say anything today that would reflect on our international relations. I have many friends in that country. But I say again that we cannot follow such a policy. I remember being in this house when my friend from Twillingate was secretary to the Right Hon. Mackenzie King. When he came to Ottawa first he was a nice looking young fellow. I remember well that when I came here first we were buying about $400 million more from the United States than we were selling them. I remember that in 1930 we were still buying over $3 million a day more. Then, after the 22 long and awful years, which Canada must have been strong to endure, with the Liberal party in power, we wind up buying from the United States $3 million to $4 million a day or over $1 billion more than we sold per year. Did that make the United States take any of our surplus wheat? Did it prompt them to buy any of the stuff we want to sell? No, politics are not run that way. Kissing may go by favours in politics but it does not do so in business.
I know there are some men in this house who have tried hard to mix business and politics but my view after some years in the house is that it is easier to mix politics into business than to put business into politics. It does not seem to me that under our democratic system there is an opportunity to get 66968-9-173
The Budget-Mr. Rowe down to cold facts. We not only have a country of tremendous size but we have built up the strongest social security and welfare state that any similar number of people have ever enjoyed, and we live beside the United States of America. Our labour unions are controlled by heads of unions in the United States. We have no hope of bringing about reductions in wages. I have listened to bank managers from coast to coast telling government to cut down wages, to cut down expenditures and you would think it was as easy as cutting Black Diamond cheese. Can we maintain this welfare state and high standard of living while at the same time accepting any reduction in our net production? No, Mr. Speaker, the only hope for this country to maintain this excessively high standard of social security compared with any similar number of people in the world is to broaden our basis of taxation, more people, more jobs, more industry and more taxpayers. That must be done if this country is to survive.
May I be pardoned for a few minutes, Mr. Speaker, if I look back a little bit into the shades of the past. I know the policy of the Liberal party of those years. I have watched a lot of it and I have read about the rest of it. The part that I watched was even worse than the part about which I read.
We know their policy down through the ages, at a time when the United States put a tariff against everything from this country except our raw products. One of the leaders of our party, and the prime minister of Canada at that time, saw a vision. He saw that this country had to do something to keep our own people employed if we were ever going to become a nation. He brought in the national policy which became the fiscal trading policy of this country. Might I say that this is a policy which has never been diverted from and this party is in power today because they told the people of Canada they intended to change the policy then in force and give employment to our own people by processing our own resources. This is the reason we are here, and the reason we will stay here for some time. This is the reason Canada will grow and prosper as our pioneering leaders expected.
I know there are those on the other side because I have heard old quiet Liberals pleading in their ridings and pleading in this house for support for tariff changes. I heard one in this house plead for tariff protection on bones, bottles and rubbers, and he was from Waterloo North. He is not here now; he did not get the protection. But we have watched this down through the years.

The Budget-Mr. Rowe The United States of America did not retaliate. They had more respect for our prime minister of that day than any other leader in Canada. In those days the Liberal party was shilly-shallying between commercial union and political absorption by that country.
A few years later the Liberals ran an election on commercial union, and thank the Lord they were defeated. A few years later they suggested reciprocity. The United States, in the meantime, had wanted our raw products. It is true that there is always a joker in the thing. Afterwards it became known that there never was a reciprocity agreement for the Canadian people for all products. There is not an hon. member within the hearing of my voice who can deny that. It was proven two months after the 1911 election that we never had been offered reciprocity except on some raw products. All we had been offered was an open door in the United States for all our raw products. Two years afterwards the new tariff that came in under the Wilson government gave us free entry for more of our products than had ever been proposed in the reciprocity agreement. We, as Conservatives, have been condemned all through the years for turning that down. It was as empty as anything could be.
Then, following that we had the Fordney-McCumber tariff. I remember that well. It resulted in an open door for our raw products. I had been selling cattle on my farm. Overnight livestock prices dropped from 22 cents a pound to 12 cents and hog prices dropped from about 18 cents per pound to 7 cents. The Fordney-McCumber tariff resulted from the fact that the farmers of the western United States saw a little depression coming up and they did not want our cattle coming into the country so they closed us out overnight. This is no discredit to them because they are running their own business. We did not howl about it or run as cry babies to Washington.
Then in 1928 or 1929 they brought in the Hawley-Smoot tariff. They needed cattle again and we sold cattle to them at 28 cents a pound. Then they closed that overnight, too, just when they saw a world depression coming. I, myself, later sold cattle for a nickel a pound. There is an old adage that there is no sentiment in business. I cannot even sell you a race horse if you do not want one, no matter how friendly we are. Do not let us kid ourselves. This goes on down through the years.
The Right Hon. Jimmy Gardiner, who was a great friend of mine and must have been a great friend of many across the way- I am not going to say he was any better than what I see over there, but he was just as good-was a marvellous politician. He never


missed a trick. Now, my dear Jimmy, since he is in the twilight of his better judgment, since he knows he is not going to return for another parliament at least, said the other day that there was no use going on with our tinkering experiments for agriculture. He told the members of the federation of agriculture that irrespective of deficiency payments on wheat, floor prices or subsidies, the only long term solution for agriculture is the development of our home markets by decentralized industry across this dominion. Oh, what a difference a few years makes. I said that 25 years ago, and he laughed at me.
Then, I should like to say a word or two about the imperial trade agreements. They were brought about by another revenue tariff brought in by the United States of America. I was here at that time. When the Right Hon. R. B. Bennett saw that he said that our only answer was to call an imperial trade conference. May I make it short, because I see my time is going. The imperial trade agreements that were brought in in 1930 have been the most misunderstood, the most underrated, the most misrepresented by the Liberal party, every one of whom condemned them, of any trade agreements that have ever been entered into by this dominion. What did they do? They fixed the situation in Europe and in England where, for instance, we were selling only five per cent of British Columbia fir timber. At that time the United States was selling over 65 per cent of the British requirements. A year after the imperial trade agreements we sold over 93 per cent and the United States sold only 6.3 per cent.
In so far as our agricultural and other products were concerned, we sold over 43 million pounds sterling during those depression years. During the next two years, with a world depression, that market increased to 71 million pounds. We saw more United States factories built in Canada in a time of depression than have ever been built in Canada by the United States even in the most lush times. This is the history, gentlemen, of this situation that we dare not ignore.
We know that the United States suffered a great body blow so far as her markets in Britain were concerned. They knew it. The result was that in 1937, after Africa had been supplying the British with oranges and grapefruit and Australia had been supplying them with other fruits, wheat, barley and other products, the United States was so desperate that the late Right Hon. Mackenzie King and his party sacrificed many of our advantages under the British preferential agreements in order to please the United States of America and make a deal by which they could draw up an Anglo-American

treaty. They were so complementary to each other that they were both signed on the same day, November 17, 1938. We surrendered the advantages that we got and left the door open for more competition in our home market.
What is the result today? In 1955, one of the last years of the Liberal government, just as they were quietly slipping out of office, we were buying $3.5 billion worth from the United States of America, and about $900 million worth of stuff that we could have manufactured here at home. United States statisticians and economists brag about the fact that they had about 700,000 people employed in the United States producing products for consumption in Canada.
Mr. Speaker, it is almost too late. It is later than we think. Canada cannot afford this any more than we can afford to compete in this cold climate with the tropical production of agricultural products. In Canada in our manufacturing industry you can take your coat off and work in your shirt sleeves when it is 50 degrees below zero. But if you try shovelling snow behind the barn when it is 40 degrees below zero and try to compete with Australia or New Zealand in the dairy industry, then you will find that we have a difficult situation.
The GATT agreements were drawn up ten years ago by the former government. Hon. C. D. Howe at that time said, "We have lowered our trade barriers; we have done more to make it possible for people to sell in Canada than has any other country in the world". When he went into the trade agreement it was like going into a gun battle after you have thrown away your gun. What happened? Is there an hon. member who can rise in his place and tell me that the general agreement on tariffs and trade has helped industry and development in this country? It has not helped one iota. The situation is similar to that in 1930 when the Liberal party wanted to have a countervailing situation. They became tired of their free trade doctrine. They wanted to have countervailing duties. The late Mr. Dunning said, "We will have a countervailing situation. If Washington raises tariffs, we will raise ours." In other words, we delegated our responsibility in fiscal matters to Washington. Then they go to Geneva.
Mr. Speaker, these problems are purely Canadian problems. This climate is purely Canadian. Our geographical situation is purely Canadian. I just want to say this. With the great forthcoming Russian competition, with Japan selling today for 40 per cent less than the United States with her mass production can supply goods in Europe, and with China selling for one-third or 30 per
66968-9-173J
The Budget-Mr. Rowe cent of the cost of our product, do you mean to tell me that the European bloc is going to solve our problems? The only place where these problems can be solved is here. They are Canadian problems and can only be solved by Canadian policies.
Whether we like it or not, I am satisfied that we are living in a different age. I have long since awakened from dreaming about the federation of the world. Some day when we are all one family, with NATO and all the rest combining in technical matters, in science and military affairs, and everybody being his brother's keeper, everything will be fine. That sounds fine and it will be fine. But when it happens, certainly some of us older ones are going to be upstairs looking down. It is going to take a long time.
But in the interval, Mr. Speaker, let us not fool ourselves. These problems are purely Canadian. We have the highest rate of cost of any people in the world per capita. We bring in more from outside the country than any other people in the world. We are recklessly extravagant because we have the greatest resources of any similar people in the world. The great St. Lawrence development, the great two systems of railways and all that they mean cost money. The only hope for lower taxes, for Canada's long term solvency and security, whether in war or in peace, is more people; and in order to get them we need more jobs and more industries. We need encouragement for those industries just as much as we need it for the farmer.
Agriculture is extremely important. When I entered this house first, 45 per cent of the people were employed in agriculture. Agriculture was the backbone of the country. I worked that "backbone" idea until everybody got tired hearing it. Today the manufacturing industry produces more national wealth and gives more employment than all of the primary industries combined, including agriculture, mining, oil wells, fishing and lumbering. I recall reading the other day a C.N.R. survey report in which it was stated that they had studied industrial centres like Joliette, Three Rivers, Stratford, Ontario, and other places-seven or eight of them-and had found on the average that 100 men employed in a plant gave 427 other jobs and meant a million dollars of retail business. Mr. Speaker, just stop and think of what we could do in our democracy.
In my closing remarks, Mr. Speaker, I just want to say that these problems are unique to Canada and must be solved in Canada. Do not let anybody tell you that during the regime of my hon. friend who just preceded me and who is temporarily at least leading the party, you led the world

The Budget-Mr. Dupuis because you did not. In ten years following the war old England-and many in their party thought that she was all through-increased her industrial activity by 48 per cent. Australia increased hers by 40 per cent. West Germany increased hers by 53 per cent. The United States increased hers by 37 per cent. We increased ours by only 25 per cent. We have fallen down. We have lagged behind the world. It is a wonder some of their friends in the other place cling to the old dusty doctrine that we have nothing to sell but our resources, that we do not know how to make things out of them.
In conclusion I would just say this, Mr. Speaker; when I see you rise I will sit down. I say this to the government in all sincerity. I have absolute confidence in this government, in the leadership and in the great battalions that is behind them with their youth and ability. But, Mr. Speaker, these are purely Canadian problems and they cannot be solved by policies fashioned in Washington or anchored in Geneva. (Translation):
