speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, you have no doubt noticed the prolonged applause that followed the speech of the hon. member for Dufferin-Simcoe (Mr. Rowe). Our friends opposite probably meant this as an expression of their great joy, because the representative who just sat down made them forget for a few minutes the intense blackness of the budget submitted last week by the hon. Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming). I can understand their rejoicing and hardly blame them for it.
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member who just sat down again recalled the years of deep darkness which, according to him, marked the period during which the Liberal party was in power. Well, as I looked at him a moment ago, standing there tall and erect, pinkcheeked, firm of voice, dapper, in a freshly-pressed suit, with a handsome tie, white silk shirt and gold watch, I said to myself: "Well those 22 years of Liberal rule were not so hard on him, after all!" Judging by his looks, I would be very very much surprised if the hon. member had suffered any hardship during those years of Liberal administration. He certainly was not brought up on dishwater and blueing.
And now, Mr. Speaker, to get back to the matter we should be considering, the budget speech. I hope the hon. member for Dufferin-Simcoe will bear me no grudge if I do not continue in the same vein as he did, harking back to remote antiquity. Before I go on, may I express the wish that he remain as healthy and jovial during the years of Conservative government that lie ahead, as he was during those of the last Liberal regime.
Mr. Speaker, last year, the hon. Minister of Finance introduced his first budget to the country; it was the first budget of his parliamentary career. When he announced small tax reductions, we said that they smacked of funerals. In fact, they had to do with cut flowers, rat poison and ambulances. Today we readily realize that, in fact, he was preparing a first class burial of all those promises and illusions which the Tories had advertised in the last election campaign.
Mr. Speaker, the budget introduced by the hon. Minister of Finance last week is one which is worthy of the last Conservative regimes, worthy of Mr. Borden, of Mr. Bennett and, 30 years hence, history will record that it was worthy of Mr. Diefenbaker. No one will escape its effects. All classes of citizens, small, medium or big, wage earners, individuals, corporations, all are affected. There is a general tax increase in all fields. And the hon. Minister of Finance, who is well known for his poise, came into the house the other night, without a quiver, and announced with a smile on his lips that the deficit was not very high, only $600 million. What a piece of news! What a great joy for the people of Canada!
However, Mr. Speaker, the hon. Minister of Finance could not help looking a bit crestfallen and his smile was a bit strained, because he introduced that evening an unprecedented peacetime deficit, a peacetime increase in taxation which we had never seen since the Borden and Bennett regimes.
Mr. Speaker, what cannot be overlooked,- and what our friends opposite forget to tell us-is that not a single promise made in the course of the last election campaign has been fulfilled. The government was elected on false promises and, today, coming as they do here to violate their promises, I say, like the whole Canadian people at present, that they do not deserve our confidence. They distorted the facts, they ignored their promises: they should then resign at once, before it is too late.
And that, Mr. Speaker, is but one instance of two years of Conservative government. What will be the situation two years hence?

maintopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: The finish!

maintopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
In all parts of the country, people say that they want a change of government. Everywhere in the streets we hear people say: "Just wait, as usual, they won't be there for long."
Yesterday evening, the hon. Secretary of State (Mr. Courtemanche) made a surprising speech. He who had promised to all and sundry that a Conservative government would mean prosperity and lower taxation, told us that in his view the Minister

of Finance's decision to boost taxes was a very wise one. Drawing a comparison, he said:	Look at France, General de Gaulle is
popular. Everything is shipshape over there and yet he has increased taxes. Therefore we are also right in raising them.
Mr. Speaker, the situation in France, when General de Gaulle took over, was different. He came at a time when that country was in a deplorable state, without a stable budget, whereas, when our friends opposite came into power, they found the country in a state of prosperity never before reached in the course of our history. And in order to make the hard pill of taxation easier to swallow, the Minister from Quebec pointed out that during his budget speech the hon. Minister of Finance had spoken in French for one minute out of two hours. That is a fine effort on his part! That is grand! We appreciate it very much, but you may be assured, Mr. Speaker, that the French population of Canada would have preferred to hear him speak English during that minute or two, if it could have served to announce lower instead of higher taxes.
Mr. Speaker, I should like to recall the promises made by our friends opposite. Oh, I know they do not like being reminded of those fine promises, advertised in the weeklies of the various constituencies they represent here, extraordinary, fantastic, astounding promises. "We shall reduce income tax." "We shall abolish the sales tax." "Under the Conservative government, nobody will suffer from unemployment." "We shall undertake huge public works projects." "We shall call at once a federal-provincial conference to solve fiscal problems." Two years have elapsed since then, and the conference has not yet been called. We are still waiting. "We shall appoint an ambassador to the Vatican." It is about time to do so. "We shall abolish the wastage of people's money." "We shall reduce the wastage in the Colombo plan." "We shall see to it that the provinces regain their autonomy in the field of education." "We shall abolish federal help to universities." "We shall increase family allowances." "We shall grant old-age pensions to people at 60." "We shall introduce an emergency measure to protect our textile industry against dumping." "We shall introduce, at the very first session, a vast farmers' assistance program." Ora pro nobis.
Mr. Speaker, all that was vision. All that was but idle promises. All that was but a joke. And, as an illustration of the monumental blunder of our friends opposite, here is a cartoon which appeared in the Toronto Star. You can see it as well as I do, since you are not very far, Mr. Speaker, just look how fine this is. Here is the Prime
The Budget-Mr. Dupuis Minister; he looks very natural. And, standing by his side, is Mr. Fleming, the present Minister of Finance. And then, you can see John Q. Public in front of both.

maintopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I hope it is not Smallwood?

maintopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
No, he is not as "small" as the hon. member who has interrupted me. And then, we have the Prime Minister of Canada inviting John Q. Public to look through a telescope, and telling him "Come and see the fine vision". Unfortunately, John Q. Public is being shown the telescope by the wrong end. And, while John Q. Public is peering through the telescope, there is a certain Mr. Fleming coming behind to tell him, while he is snatching John Q. Public's wallet: "Now, come here my child." And John Q. Public is standing before the Minister of Finance who says to him:
(Text):
Come and see the nice vision.
(Translation):
And, Mr. Speaker, it is regrettable that we may not copy that cartoon, because, frankly, more than one Canadian would find it singularly timely. May I put it on the record, Mr. Speaker?
A few moments ago I referred to some fantastic promises made by our friends opposite, but we should not forget that in addition to not fulfilling those promises, they took the same action they had condemned in the past.
Last winter, I was listening to a French television program, and I had the pleasure of seeing the Minister of Finance with the hon. member for Chapleau (Mr. Martel) sitting on his right and the hon. member for Dorchester (Mr. Drouin) on his left. It was really something to see! The hon. member for Dorchester had in his hand a small sheet of paper and, turning towards the minister, as we used to do at school during the rhetoric class, he said: "Mr. Fleming, is it not true that the country is going through a period of amazing development?" And Mr. Fleming replied: "Yes indeed, we will restore the nation's prestige." Then the hon. member for Chapleau asked. "Is it not true, Mr. Finance Minister, that the country has been waiting a long time for the return to power of the Conservatives?" "Indeed", replied the Minister of Finance, "Canada will be going through years of prosperity such as it has never known."
Well, Mr. Speaker, that was a program for political meetings, a monumental hoax, a television program, a huge joke, all lies and false promises.

The Budget-Mr. Dupuis
The other night, the Minister of Finance recalled in this house a little story which, he thought, was most original. This is what the Minister of Finance told us on March 30, 1953:
I speak as one who does not smoke and who is not personally affected by this present bill.
We were considering the excise tax bill on cigarettes, and the hon. member went on to say:
But as a non-smoker, I wish to say that I think the taxes on cigarettes and tobacco are still too high. I wish to say also that, if we have a smuggling problem at the border today with respect to cigarettes it is largely the creation of this government by its boosting sky-high of excise taxes and other impositions on cigarettes, particularly the large advances in taxes that were made two years ago.
Now, when the Minister of Finance was just an opposition backbencher, he used to attack the Liberal government which was then having budgetary surpluses, saying that, when the government wanted to raise the excise tax on cigarettes, it was contributing to inflation.
Well, Mr. Speaker, the same Minister of Finance came to us the other evening, well groomed, with a nice Fleming smile, to announce that he proposed to increase the excise tax on cigarettes. What promises! What results! What disappointment! And, just do not try to tell the Minister of Finance that he was wrong! Oh! no, his budget is a fine one, the deficit is only $600 million. He will not accept any comments, nor any criticism. He knows where he is going.
He reminds me, Mr. Speaker, of the Pharisee in the Gospel who exclaims: "I thank Thee, Lord, that I am not like other men. I do not smoke, I do not drink, nor am I the same type of minister of finance as my predecessor, having never indulged in too many surpluses."
Mr. Speaker, there is also another member, now a minister in the cabinet of our friends opposite, who made the following statement, as reported on page 492 of Hansard for October 29, 1951. Here is the statement made at the time by the hon. member for Three Rivers, who is now the Solicitor General (Mr. Balcer):
Finally, another means the government has found to meet the rising cost of living is the setting up of an additional cigarette tax-truly an unduly high tax. I submit that the government is now inducing the Canadian people to become the greatest smugglers in the world.
Mr. Speaker, not only is the present Conservative government driving Canadians to become the greatest smugglers in the world, -when people are starving, you never know what they can do-but it is driving the country back into the dark days of the former Conservative government.
Moreover, Mr. Speaker, I should like to remind the Minister of Finance that, when he was in the opposition, he blamed the Liberal government for daring to increase the 4 per cent tax levied by Bennett, namely the federal sales tax. And here we have, as Minister of Finance the same man who, in the past, would shout and rant against an increase in the sales tax and declare that if the Conservatives were elected to office, they would remove that evil tax which was creating inflation in Canada.
Here is part of a remarkable speech made by the Minister of Finance when he was in the opposition. Discussing the sales tax, he said this:
(Text):
This tax still applies on clothing, boots and shoes, furniture, some processed foods, all of which are basic necessities of life. Is it any wonder that today we are not very far away from the danger of recurring inflation? X do not believe even the minister will stand up in this house and say that the danger of inflation has passed. Then why does the minister insist on heaping up these indirect taxes which have such an inflationary effect. They boost the cost of living; they reduce the value of savings and insurance and make more difficult the lot of those who are trying to procure housing for themselves. This budget lost a great opportunity to do something for the people with small means or small incomes in neglecting to reduce the sales tax.
(Translation) :
Well, Mr. Speaker, last week, despite all the promises that he had made, the same Minister of Finance who was then opposed to sales tax informed us without flinching, that he was now increasing the sales tax which he condemned in the past.
Moreover, Mr. Speaker, I have here a quotation of the man who is the present Prime Minister. Here is what he said on February 15, 1954, about the new sales tax:
(Text):

And they dare today raise the sales tax!
When the hon. Secretary of State (Mr. Courtemanche) made a speech last night, did he refer to the appointment of an ambassador to the Vatican, he who had so insistently urged the Liberal government to take such a step? Did he refer to that matter, he who, during the last election campaign in the province of Quebec used to blame the Liberal government for not having appointed one while all recognized countries in the world have their ambassador there? If last night the Secretary of State had been consistent, he would have repeated what he said in the House of Commons at the time the Liberals were governing the country. I quote from page 553 of Hansard of March 18, 1952, where I find what he said then:

maintopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
But X wonder why Canada goes on ignoring the existence of the Vatican, where the other great nations of the world, nations which sometimes count an infinitely small minority of Catholics make a point of being represented by an ambassador or other official envoy.
Well, Mr. Speaker, I do say this to the Secretary of State, to the Minister of Finance, and to the Prime Minister: You promised to reduce taxes, but you did nothing; you promised to balance the budget and you give us a budget showing a deficit of $600 million; you promised to abolish taxes on cigarettes and you increased them; you promised to abolish the sales tax, and you increased it; you promised to name an ambassador to the Vatican and you do not talk about it any more; you have repeatedly deceived all the people of Canada.
Mr. Speaker, as far as corporation tax is concerned, the Minister of Finance, when he used to sit on this side of the house, had this to say:
(Text):
What were the effects of the increases last year in the corporation taxes? They were passed on wherever possible and the effect was inflationary, as it added to the cost of living.
(Translation) :
And, Mr. Speaker, during the discussion of the budget in 1952, and still in the same speech, Mr. Fleming told us as we can see on page 1535 of the official record of April 23, that the increase in corporation taxes automatically brought about a raise in rail and telephone rates.
Well, Mr. Speaker, even before the present hon. Minister of Finance announced an increase in corporation taxes, the Bell Telephone Company has been allowed-under a Conservative government and without consulting Parliament-to increase its rates while railway companies are increasing their freight rates.
The Budget-Mr. Dupuis
And, Mr. Speaker, there are still people in the province, in this country and even here, who attempt to discredit a government that was a thousand times better than the present administration of this country.
I now refer to another page of Hansard where I find a statement made by the present Minister of Finance on March 12, 1952, as may be seen on page 375:
(Text):
I may say that the time has come-and this is my final word-
(Translation):
It seems, Mr. Speaker, that his last word has not been spoken yet.
(Text):
Mr. Speaker-when this government should be told to let the people handle their own money. We want to develop the resources of this country. We have to have capital. That capital must come from the savings of the people and from profits. We must have that kind of capital. We must have savings. We cannot have them if the government is going to go on fleecing the people of this country by gouging them with these heavy taxes. We are depending today far too heavily on foreign capital for the development of these resources. We want to see more Canadian capital going into the development of our own Canadian resources. We must have increased savings. We must have increased earnings in Canada. We cannot have those as long as the weight of federal taxation in this country is so seriously retarding Canadian enterprises.
(Translation):
And the same Minister of Finance has completely changed his mind since he has been in office. Not only does he not abolish the corporation income tax, which helps increase the cost of living and creates inflation, but the Minister of Finance, solemn and unflinching, stands there proudly to announce that his Conservative government is increasing that tax which he had previously denounced.
There are other passages which I could quote, and which show what he thought of the then government, for instance his statement of March 3, 1955, but which he now denies.
Mr. Speaker, need I recall all those things? There is not a single Canadian who does not know how the Conservatives betrayed their good faith during the general election. How many promises were made which remained a dead letter? The hon. member for Three Rivers who is now the Solicitor General, rose in the house in 1956 and blamed the Liberal government for its failure to raise family allowances. It was the same minister who travelled through the province of Quebec in the last elections, making speeches in favour of our friends opposite. He would say: "We Conservatives have some consideration

The Budget-Mr. Dupuis for large families, and we will increase family allowances." Have they been raised? No.
The only increases we have seen since the budget was laid down have been tax increases, in short increases of every kind, but never an increase in social welfare benefits. Those were false promises, misleading words to hoodwink the electorate.
Mr. Speaker, a while ago I heard my friend the hon. member for Dufferin-Simcoe claim that the Liberals had done nothing for this country. I suppose they did nothing in the field of social welfare! No social legislation was passed by the Conservatives. The legislation concerning old age pension, the blind, the disabled, unemployment insurance, family allowances, was enacted by the Liberals and gave something to the people.
In regard to the sovereignty of this country, did the Liberal party not go forward? Under the able guidance of the Right Hon. Louis S. St. Laurent, did the Liberal party not give Canada a sovereignty which was unknown before? At this stage, I only want to mention some of the measures passed by the Liberal government, which have brought about the recognition of the sovereignty of this country: the Canadian Citizenship Act, a Liberal achievement; the abolition of appeals to the London Privy Council, a Liberal achievement; the repatriation of the Canadian constitution, a Liberal achievement; the appointment of a Canadian governor general, the establishment of a Royal Military College in the province of Quebec, the setting up of an autonomous Canadian military force, all those were Liberal achievements.
In the administrative field, the Liberal party has given this country the finest years of prosperity ever enjoyed by Canada. Under the administration of Sir Wilfrid Laurier, whose policy we are proud to continue; under the guidance of the Right Hon. William Lyon Mackenzie King whom we respect and venerate as a great Canadian leader; under the guidance also of the Right Hon. Louis St. Laurent, this little French Canadian from Compton, who made this country famous throughout the world, the Liberal party has endowed Canada with a prosperous administration. It is claimed in this house that the Liberal party did nothing for 22 years. Everything the Liberal party did has been of benefit to those very people who, today, talk with indescribable ingratitude.
Mr. Speaker, through the fault of those same people who misled us and abused the Canadian voters, with the help of the Duplessis administration which our friends hold in such high esteem, every year, in the province of Quebec we are losing-I am referring to the
[Mr. Dupuis.1

federal field-millions of dollars we should be receiving from the federal treasury. The citizens of Quebec pay taxes just as the rest of the country, and they too contribute to the country's development, but when the time comes to receive their fair share of the money they have paid out, and which should be distributed to all Canadian provinces, it is another matter. This through the fault of those very people who are now facing us from the opposite side of the house, and who lied shamelessly in the last elections, saying to the people: "Vote for us, the Duplessist candidates, and when we get to Ottawa, things will change. You want an ambassador to the Vatican? He will be leaving the next morning." Apparently, he has not yet taken the boat.
The same people also declared: "We will abolish grants to universities". What a farce! Have the grants been abolished? On the contrary, they were rapidly increased. What a bunch of jokers!
They also promised to put an end to contributions to the Colombo plan. And, Mr. Speaker, it was quite a sight to see the publicity we were subjected to in Quebec, with full pages in daily and weekly newspapers: "The Liberals give to the Colombo plan; Mr. Duplessis gives to his province". Those same people travelled throughout the province making this statement:	"Vote for us,
send us to Ottawa, we will straighten things out and bring back the taxpayers' money given away to the Colombo plan". Once in power, they do not get the taxpayers' money back from the Colombo plan; instead of that, they allocate even more of the taxpayers' money toward the Canadian contribution to the Colombo plan. Liars! Whited sepulchres! Pharisees!
Every year the province of Quebec loses millions of dollars by refusing to accept federal grants for the building of the trans-Canada highway and help to universities and other federal grants in different fields, when taxpayers in my province are paying the same taxes as any other Canadian taxpayer.
Well, Mr. Speaker, we, the Liberals, want to live as Canadians, we are proud of being Canadians and I will point out the great difference between the Conservative party and the Liberal party. The Liberal party is a national party with a single concept, a single thought and a single national philosophy.
Chameleon-like, the Conservative party changes its color or philosophy according to its environment. Go out west, you would hear a speech prepared for people of that part of our country. But, in Quebec, the speech is altogether different.

Well, Mr. Speaker, I would rather be a member of a truly Canadian party, such as the Liberal party. We, Liberals, are in favour of the Colombo plan and we never said otherwise.
We also hold that the rights of the French language should be respected. You will never be able to quote a Liberal member as saying anything in this house against the French language. However, we have heard an Ontario member, on the Conservative or Tory side, remind us that it was one of the privileges we owed the Freemasons to be able to speak French in this country.
Such statements are vicious and unfortunate and they undermine national unity.
Mr. Speaker, you have never heard any Liberal member come out against "O Canada" as the national anthem. However, within the Conservative party, two ministers-quite candidly, suddenly, without thinking it over, and without any question having been asked- said that they were against "O Canada" as a national anthem.
Mr. Speaker, before closing, I might say that the Liberal party has given Canada a solid doctrine, and a Canadian citizenship that is recognized everywhere. And this brings back to my mind the trip made abroad by the Right Hon. Mr. St. Laurent. I recall that when he walked into Notre Dame cathedral in Paris-the story was reported at length in all newspapers-when this grand old man with silver hair walked down the central aisle, the grand organ of the cathedral broke into "O Canada, our Home and Native Land", That, Mr. Speaker, was a great day in our history.
We are now living in troubled times, that of the Conservative regime, which take us back to the dark years of the Bennetts and Bordens. Two years in power, and all promises broken. I shall now take them one by one, and you will note that all of them were broken. Instead of administering the country, they will joke about the whole thing.
The Conservatives had promised to reduce the income tax; they increased it. They have promised to abolish the sales tax; they increased it.
They also said that nobody would suffer from unemployment. I need not say more on this count.
They said they would undertake huge public works projects. Those are still to come.
They had promised-that was in 1957- to call a federal-provincial conference at once. I feel they are not very anxious to do so, lest they be criticized by the provincial delegates.

They had promised to appoint an ambassador to the Vatican. As I said a few moments ago, he hasn't taken the boat yet.
There was also a promise with regard to restricting the waste of the people's money, comprising aid under the Colombo plan; now the Canadian contribution has been raised.
We had been promised provincial autonomy in matters of education; our friends from the province of Quebec just voted an increase in the assistance given to the universities.
We had also been promised a raise of family allowances; we are still waiting for the Solicitor General, that fatherly minister, to do so.
There had been a promise of old age pensions from age 60; there are now citizens who are 62, 63 and even 64, but they are still waiting.
We had also been promised an emergency act to protect the textile industry against dumping; we are still waiting for that.
We were also told of plans to launch a vast program to help our farmers; that is still to come.
Mr. Speaker, all hon. members have the duty to denounce that phantom budget which has deceived the good faith of our voters and to tell this country right out: "The Conservatives have made promises which they did not keep, they have mentioned a vision for which you are paying dearly today. Wake up before it is too late."

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is indeed a pleasure to have this opportunity to take part in the budget debate. I remember having my name on the list last year and the debate concluding before I had the opportunity to congratulate the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) on his budget. Almost a year has passed since then and we are now in a good position to assess his achievement in last year's budget. I recall the expenditures it provided for such things as home building, a program that took approximately $550 million out of the treasury of Canada last year; the millions of dollars approved to improve the condition of the aged, the blind and the incapacitated; the supplementary payments to the maritime provinces to support their recovery after 22 years of Liberal rule; and the grain assistance payments to the farm people of the prairie provinces.
As the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River (Mr. Benidickson) indicated on budget night,

The Budget-Mr. Nasserden the present budget is a record-breaking one for peacetime or wartime expenditures. Last year his criticism of the budget was that it was not planned. This year his criticism of the budget is that it was not planned. Last year he said it "growed". This year he said that "it only happened". He has not changed his tune very much, though he was somewhat subdued in his criticism this year and his whole attitude indicated that he was not eager to indicate that there would be a million unemployed this year or that there would be a billion dollar deficit as he indicated last year.
When all arguments of logic failed him he drew on the reconversion loan of last summer, garnished it with the bond market weakness in the United States of America and came up with the significant question as to why the government is not undertaking a study as is being undertaken in the United States with regard to the outstanding bond market weakness there. Any third grade student could have told him that the government foresaw conditions and launched the reconversion loan drive rather opportunely to protect the refinancing of Canada's war loan maturities which were products of the Liberal government during wartime.
When the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River and his colleagues mentioned bad faith, lower taxes and increased expenditures for services they display some of that old spirit of degenerate Liberalism that convinced the Canadian people it was time for a change. When the hon. member for Bonavista-Twil-lingate (Mr. Pickersgill) referred to the Right Hon. Louis St. Laurent's remarks with regard to how they kept their pledges, which the hon. member said were implemented in full, he even went so far as to say that he was proud of that proud boast. He called that kind of record the ultimate in good faith. He indeed has my sympathy; indeed, all his colleagues have my sympathy. It must be humiliating to them to see many of their favorite election pledges being brought into being by a Tory government. I think of such things as the South Saskatchewan river dam, not endorsed by Louis St. Laurent but long a promise of Liberal members of the House of Commons at election time. The reality of this project now taking shape must certainly take on the aspect of a vision to many of those who were in the front benches of the Liberal party. It is not the kind of vision that the Liberals scoffed at so scornfully last year but one which brings vividly to their minds thoughts of opportunities lost and dreams shattered but not entirely forgotten.
I think of health insurance, long a plank in Liberal platforms but today a living thing


put in force by a government that tries to keep its promises, and in this instance a Liberal platform promise also that goes back to 1919. I would have mentioned the history of the old age pension fund but the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Nowlan) took the Liberals down a path that they hoped had been forgotten as he traced the utterances of the Hon. Douglas Abbott on the financing of that fund.
No wonder the financial critic of the opposition was subdued in his criticism. He knows that the government is today proposing expenditures of $1,212 million for the municipalities and the provinces compared with an expenditure of $689 million in the year 1956-57. When he complains that almost every pocket is hit let him remember that the main increases in the budget fall on purchases of tobacco and whisky, plus the increases in corporation taxes. Would he care to offer any alternative sources of revenue? To be perfectly frank, he did not attempt to perform the good offices of an opposition critic. He went back to defend the 1954 Liberal budget and well he might, for Canadians remember that that was about the time that things began to get difficult for them.
The C.C.F. critic has not learned much since a year ago. Like the rest of his colleagues, he labels everything under consideration as misleading if it does not give him the opportunity and cause to criticize the government. The C.C.F. have always hated the man who leaves a good estate and once again they have expressed that hatred by calling for a capital gains tax and lower interest rates. Anyone who is interested in the history of economics knows that the greatest benefactors of capital gains are widows and orphans and the retired men and women of a country. The C.C.F. would deny these people the benefits of a decent rate of interest on their sole source of income in many cases, an odd way to practise, "humanity first."
I was pleased to hear the hon. member for Hull (Mr. Caron) recall the by-election in the province of Quebec. We on this side of the house are thankful to the people of that riding for the confidence they expressed in last year's activity by sending to the house the hon. member for Montmagny-L'lslet (Mr. Fortin). On several occasions the hon. member for Hull has expressed fear of the guillotine being used in the civil service. His friends in the civil service remember the ruthlessness of the Liberal axe which in many cases brought them to their positions in the employment of this government. The hon. member is really

disappointed because he cannot go out and point to the guillotine as a weapon used by this government on the civil service of this country. You know, sir, if we wanted to solve unemployment the way the Liberals would do had they come to power as we came to power, we would fire half a million civil servants and hire those who are unemployed today. The civil service employees in Canada never had a better champion than John Diefenbaker and this government. In so far as appointments are concerned, no one can say that this government has taken what could be called anything approaching a partisan stand. To be quite frank, I think this government has been entirely too generous with many of the people in the public service of Canada who do not appreciate that there has been a change of government. Some of these people still think that orders come from Liberal headquarters.
The hon. member for Hull has a well-known theme song. "I blame the Tory government", he says. He says the national debt has gone up, but he failed to mention that the per capita debt is down. He estimated that we would have a million unemployed last year, but we had only half a million. He said we are trying to get by with impossible promises. Impossible they may have been to the Liberals, but this government is fulfilling the very promises the Liberal government reneged upon. The hon. member for Gloucester (Mr. Robichaud) is a real Liberal. He asked the question, what real and significant changes in government have taken place? He answered the question in the negative and then proceeded to cite everything that this government has done. He drew a picture of large surpluses of primary products, and then retreated from that statement by saying that time did not allow him to elaborate upon it.
The hon. member was so bold as to say that this government had failed to show waste and extravagance in the departments of government, forgetting the printing bureau in Hull. He asserted that this government had refused to meet the provinces and municipalities to discuss their problems. Where has the hon. member been during the last several months? The fact of the matter is that we have not any opposition in the opposition today. Every last one of them admires the government and the courageous action it has been taking since coming to office. They admire the Minister of Finance and his budget. They know Canadians were expecting a balanced budget and the taxes involved. They know that this budget struck a happy balance in meeting the problems of unemployment and inflation. They have my sympathy I assure you, Mr. Speaker, 66968-9-1744
The Budget-Mr. Nasserden and they will need more than that to recapture the imagination of the Canadian people.
In weak, subdued voices they say this budget was not planned, it only happened. Let us take a look at the record. It only happened to provide the greatest home building program in the history of this nation. This program provided homes on convenient terms and provided employment to the construction and allied trades of Canada. Second, unemployment benefits were provided on a scale and in a measure hitherto unequalled in the history of this country-not planned, it only happened. There is no $6 Harris in this government, but pensions are provided to meet the needs of Canadians.
The refinancing of Canada's wartime bonds was a measure that restored individual interest in these transactions. Hospital insurance, the dream of Liberals since 1919, was enacted under a Conservative government. It was certainly not planned, it only happened under a Conservative government. The $25 million in supplementary payments to the maritimes was certainly not planned by the Liberals. It only happened under a Diefenbaker government. The $13.5 million to Newfoundland was certainly not planned, but it is certainly happening. The university grants were raised from $16 million to $26 million, and that was not planned by the Liberals. It only happened under a Tory government. The $41,300,000 for prairie grain growers was not planned, it only happened under a Conservative government.
The hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Argue) has insinuated that the new members from Saskatchewan and western Canada did not even know where to hang their hats when they arrived in Ottawa last May. I am willing to admit that that may have been so. When we came to Ottawa last May we were so green that we threw our hats down in the centre of the map of Saskatchewan, and when we picked them up the people of Saskatchewan found $100 million voted so that there would be a dam across the South Saskatchewan river at Outlook. This was the first step taken in recent years to correct the inequities of those policies of the Liberal party which had resulted in giving everything to the people of other provinces and making the people of Saskatchewan the poor relations of those other parts of Canada.
We knew so little about where to hang our hats that we threw them in a pile over the Prairie Farm Assistance Act, and when we reached for them that act was amended to provide benefits to more people who needed those benefits than at any time before in our history. We were so green that we thought a man who contributed to the 1 per cent
2730	HOUSE OF
The Budget-Mr. Nasser den levy should be able to benefit, and today many who were denied payments under the former regulations are now eligible for payments in the event of crop failure. There are still some improvements that could be made in that act.
As I intimated earlier, one of the great needs in all areas of Canada is better housing. When we came to parliament a year ago we found the National Housing Act on the table, and it looked like a good place to hang our hats. When we picked up our hats we found that the government of Canada had voted $300 million to be repaid on convenient terms. This legislation has been of great help to people in all parts of Canada; in the cities and towns as well as the farm areas. There has been one notable exception, and that is in Saskatchewan where farmers are denied the use of this legislation because of the so-called farm security act introduced by the C.C.F. in Saskatchewan. If the hon. member for Assiniboia knew where to hang his hat he would hang it on the farm security act and give Saskatchewan farmers the same benefits as are available to farmers in other provinces. At the beginning of this session we voted another $250 million for housing, and these programs have been of great help to those engaged in carpentry and other seasonal trades.
When we came to Ottawa we found the table covered with the promises of the government of Canada to repay those millions of dollars borrowed from the people of Canada during wartime. We threw our hats over those promises and when we picked them up the people who had put their money into bonds to finance the war effort were able to get a little better return on their investment, in keeping with the increased cost of living since these bonds were first purchased. It has been said by the C.C.F. that some companies and banks have benefited from this action. I ask you, sir, is there anything we can do that will benefit those who should benefit that will not, in some way, benefit those who may not need the benefits?
We threw our hats over the excise tax and tariff regulations. We did not like trade restrictions any better than anyone else, and we removed the excise tax on a number of items, including rat poison. The hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate (Mr. Pickers-gill) has not yet told us in this house how it came about that a Liberal government had been in power for 22 years and still had an excise tax on rat poison.
On many occasions industry has come to ask for protection from the government of Canada and the people of Canada and they are usually accompanied by labour. That so-called free trader, Stanley Knowles, has often


pressed the case for protection for those engaged in labour in the factories of our country. We thought that we should protect those jobs and granted some of the requests made. When the Prime Minister (Mx. Diefenbaker) asked labour to hold the line, what was the answer that Stanley Knowles gave? It was that labour must continue to ask for increased wages and benefits. Instead of hanging his hat on that one, the hon. member for Assiniboia has sought to build for himself a free trade reputation among farmers while giving labour encouragement to continue the upward spiral of costs of everything that the farmer must buy.
There are a number of towns in Canada which are wholly dependent upon the gold mining industry for their existence. For several years now the government of Canada has been subsidizing the price of gold. It appeared that all parties were agreed on the need of some action along this line last session in order to protect these people from the disaster of shutdowns. Why does the hon. member for Assiniboia go to the farm people in the province of Saskatchewan and criticize the subsidy to the gold mining communities while he was content to see it passed here in the House of Commons? I ask you, Mr. Speaker, what his criticism would have been if we had abandoned those people and let them be shut out. He would have called us the enemy of labour and the enemy of mankind.
We hung our hats on pensions of one kind or another and voted money that belonged to the people of Canada so that some of our citizens could enjoy their retired years, their blind years or handicapped years with a little bit less anxiety. The C.C.F. say that we should have voted more. But in this debate they have criticized the budget for taxing in order to secure these revenues.
Up to the time we came to office freight rates had increased by 120 per cent during the preceding ten-year period. The government of those days allowed those increases without once assuring the Canadian people and the western farmer in particular that the Crowsnest pass rates would be protected. Last fall everyone seemed to be agreed that the non-operating employees needed an increase in wages and benefits. This government allowed that increase and we hung our hats on it too with the assurance of a subsidy to alleviate the full burden of that increase. The question of freight rates was placed under study in order to seek a solution that would eliminate the inequities of today and the Prime Minister assured parliament and the people of Canada that the Crowsnest pass rates would be protected.

When we came to Ottawa we found the biggest surplus of wheat in our entire history, a surplus that had accumulated during 12 years of Liberal rule. We threw our hats on that pile of wheat and the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Churchill) sold more wheat than anyone in this house thought could be sold. He did this at a time when every other exporting country in the entire world was unable to maintain its volume of sales. The Minister of Trade and Commerce did not wait for the customers to call. He went out and sold wheat, and when he could not sell it he gave it away to those who could not pay for it. He did this after the treasury of Canada had secured the consent of parliament to pay for this western wheat which was to be given away.
When the delegation from western Canada was here about a month ago they reminded us that when the Liberals had been in power they had given wheat to Britain at less than cost for two years, and that the government of that day had been unable to secure anything in return for this concession. Those people from western Canada estimated that this Liberal policy had cost the western grain grower something less than $600 million at that time. We voted $45 million to move wheat to underdeveloped countries during the next three years. Most of this surplus wheat is in the province of Saskatchewan. Hence even the C.C.F. must admit that we did not forget the western wheat grower when we went out and sold his surplus so that at the end of this crop year we hope to be in the position of having cleaned up stocks on farms across the prairies.
When we came down to Ottawa last spring we found a bill for over $2 million on the table to complete the payments to those who had delivered oats to the Canadian wheat board. We threw our hats on the table and voted the money. But we left our hats on that table and the government of Canada today does not have to pick up a bill for $2 million on the sale of oats. The final payment will come through in the amount of anywhere from three cents to seven cents per bushel. Where would the Liberal party hang their hats on that one, when they remember reducing the initial payment on oats by five cents a bushel at a time when farm costs were rising as they had never risen previously.
When we came to Ottawa we found on the table the representations of farm organizations in western Canada for an equitable share of the national income. We hung our hats on that problem and we searched out the causes which had led to wheat being surplus in such quantities that farmers for many years had to bear the cost of carrying
The Budget-Mr. Nasserden that wheat, which cost amounted to 12 cents per bushel. We saw how the failure of the former government to use its price support legislation for livestock products had driven many of our farmers into straight grain growing on increasingly larger acreages, because for eight years wheat and coarse grains were practically the only products in Canada that had a steady guaranteed initial price. We saw how failure to attend to markets had gradually forced many of those in the grain growing industry into other crops in order to secure cash on which to live.
We knew that farmers in western Canada were in a difficult position since 1953. There was every indication that we would be unable to bring our long term legislation before parliament soon enough last year to touch their position. We believe that these farmers wanted the causes dealt with, so that a program could be built for those who will farm in the future. We did not go back to pay for the inequities that were suffered under a Liberal administration. Instead, we sought to bring before parliament with all haste, compatible with good, sound legislation, those things which farm organizations had been asking for over a long period of years.
We took a good, long, hard look at the report of the royal commission on rural life which had been authorized by the provincial government in Saskatchewan. We were influenced by its study of farm problems. When we hung our hats on the federal treasury and secured over $40 million we made sure that those who needed it most would not be forgotten when the cheques were put in the mail. We paid it out on an acreage basis. We believed that this was a sound way to help the income position of western farmers, without aggravating the trend toward larger grain farms and the encouragement of wheat production. The delegation which came to Ottawa rejected acreage payments as charity and a handout, as something they did not want. The C.C.F. down the last two years encouraged them in that stand. They asked for an expenditure of an estimated $300 million. I do not hesitate at all in saying that if we were to spend $300 million I would feel compelled, from my knowledge of the problems in my constituency and in the province from which I come, to support payments on an acreage basis. Payments under that system would give $1,500 to the average farmer, instead of giving the larger producer $4,500 and letting the smaller farmer shift for himself. The acreage payment, whatever the amount of money involved, will benefit the smaller and average sized farmer a great deal and will still be of some help to the larger producer.
2732	HOUSE OF
The Budget-Mr. Nasserden
There is a clear cut issue at stake here as between ourselves and the C.C.F. They have come out supporting bushel payments. That can mean only one thing: They support the idea of paying $4,500 to some and practically nothing to others. I urge this government and those on the treasury benches to complete the task which was begun 12 months ago to build a truly national policy for those engaged in agriculture, a policy which will encourage the production of livestock and diversified crops on those farms where the family type of operation makes this possible. A policy such as this will give those who must of necessity produce grain, a market for that grain, and a market that will absorb their production a little more readily than has been the case during the last 13 years.
To accomplish these things I feel we must get our long term legislation dealing with credit and crop insurance passed by parliament in this session. In addition, we will need short term help, such as the acreage payment was last year. I therefore urge another acreage payment this year. I also want to emphasize how disturbed and disappointed I was when the delegation came to Ottawa and rejected acreage payments as unwanted and unappreciated by those who farm in western Canada. I am convinced from my trip during the Easter recess and from the letters which I have received that those who have made these assertions do not speak for the majority of the farmers of my constituency or for the majority of the farmers in the province of Saskatchewan. Together with those from Alberta and Manitoba I urge this government to endorse and put into operation a two-price system to cover domestically consumed wheat, the basis of which we sought to lay last year during the debates and the caucuses. Then there is the subsidy on export flour which I feel should be borne by the treasury of Canada.
The speaker who preceded me had some very interesting things to say. He said among other things that the most beautiful years of prosperity that Canada ever knew had been given to Canada by the Liberal party. There is only one thing wrong with that statement, and that is the picture of war in all its horror. The hon. member should study humility when he makes such statements. He also went on to say that the Liberal party was the only national party. I ask hon. members of the Liberal party, how many provinces do they draw their support from today in this House of Commons?
In conclusion I may say that I could not possibly support the amendment or the subamendment. These appear to be the product of confused thinking. These members of the opposition who have been hoping against


hope for a million unemployed and a billion dollar deficit have expressed their frustrations in these weak, meek and mediocre terms. They will go through the motions of proposing these amendments, but their hearts are not in them at all, and I extend to the hon. Minister of Finance and through him to the government and the Prime Minister my confidence in the main motion.

speechtext:
But to isolate our position as being something special or unusual seems to me a little unfair. All we did throughout was to identify ourselves, as I understand it, with the justice of the presentation, and of course we have nothing to be ashamed of in that particular regard.
The Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Nowlan) made the most interesting remarks in so far as his budget speech debate is concerned. I only wish he had not spoiled them by bringing in something at the end in connection with a point which has always rather bothered me, and that was the tremendous concern of politicians to hold other politicians to election promises. With a cavalier air which is quite suited to his manner, he tended to dismiss this and say, I take it, that under the exigencies of power you could not always carry out your election promises. This would have been fine, I think, if he had stopped at that rather frank admission, but of course he had to go on and ride the Grits and we got dragged into the thing, as did the hidden report. The hidden report type of argument seems to me to confuse the issue. I think if this government has not lived up to its election promises, as the Minister of National Revenue indicated it had not, it might be better if one of the cabinet ministers, especially the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming), indicated where it did not live up to its election promises.
I know that a small matter about which we have had an explanation which satisfies me is this. The Prime Minister (Mr. Diefen-baker), in speaking in Quebec during the last election, was all for support prices for farm

cut pulp wood. We have also had an explanation from the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Harkness) about the difficulties of applying this particular policy, and certainly in this particular case it seemed quite logical and reasonable. But I have never really heard the candid admission that this was one election promise which was over-extended and perhaps one which should not have been made.
One of the interesting points about the budget presentation was the indication that the Minister of Finance expects that the financial picture of the Canadian National Railways is going to improve in the next year. It seems to me that this is one of the most important organizations which has any link with the government. We have all noticed reports in the press today which indicate that Canadian National Railways have incurred a deficit of over $50 million, and in addition we have all received copies of the latest annual report. This deficit represents a sharp increase compared with last year. It is a very serious situation, most of all, I think, because one of the consequences is going to be more and more mud-slinging at the C.N.R. as being a typically inefficient public enterprise not able to hold up its end in competition with a private enterprise organization, the Canadian Pacific Railway.
It seems to me that we never recognize sufficiently that the particular burdens placed upon the C.N.R. prevent it operating in the way the C.P.R. is able to operate. That is a point which I hope all hon. members will keep in mind during the coming year, because this is a subject which is going to be very much to the fore, with discussions on freight rates and a royal commission on transportation or some other kind of inquiry into transportation going on. It seems to me that we should be well advised to do something which I suggested we should do some time ago, namely make up our minds whether we ought to go on any longer with the anachronism of one railway system operating under private enterprise within a legal framework which extends to another railroad which we cannot expect to operate on such a basis because it is saddled with so many services and so many lines which have probably never been profitable or never will be paying in any competitive sense. It seems to me that this is one of the key places where we shall need to do some thinking, and that is one of the key places where we can expect or hope for leadership.
One of the disappointing features of this budget as far as a large group in our area, or their representatives, are concerned, was the failure of the minister to make any change in the income tax rates in so far as they apply to workers in the woods. We have still
The Budget-Mr. Fisher not been able to devise any satisfactory way by means of which workers in the woods can take advantage of the amendment brought in to bring relief to those engaged in the building industry, and the fact remains that the amendment which was brought in applies only to a very small section of people actually engaged in construction work in this country. They are getting relief, whereas those who worked in the logging industry have been excluded from the benefits of this provision. I firmly believe that if the basis of good taxation law is equity, if the minister will not extend the benefit that he is giving to the construction workers to the loggers he should take it away from the construction workers. That may seem a little revolutionary, but the situation which exists at the present time is certainly not good in equity.
I was very interested when this budget came down to note the increases which had been made in corporate taxes, increases with which I have no quarrel. However, I was disappointed in one respect. Hon. members may recall that some time ago a very vocal statement was made by a pulp and paper concern which is, perhaps, the largest pulp and paper group in Ontario-the Abitibi Company-through its president when he presented his annual report. It was a continuation of a charge he had made previously about the burden of corporate taxation on the pulp and paper industry.
I should like to reiterate that in this particular field the minister is not being fair to two groups-one is the group of people who are trying to introduce proper silvicultural management into this country, and the other is the workers who are engaged in this industry, particularly in my area. We have often been faced in Ontario with the argument that we have the highest cost wood in the world because we have the highest wages. In the arguments between the workers and the company it is always being said that the company cannot pay any more, that a ceiling has been reached. I was interested the other day in reading the figures put out by the Anglo-Newfoundland Development Company with regard to their wood costs which appear in a letter in the last issue of the periodical Saturday Night from an Anglo-Newfoundland Development Company official, indicating that the per cord cost at the mill runs between $22 and $23. Anyone who is familiar with wood costs in so far as pulp is concerned will recognize that our costs in Ontario are $10 or $15 above those faced by the Anglo-Newfoundland Development Company.
One of the arguments used by the forest corporations-and they have tended to make it stick-is that unless there is a different attitude in so far as corporate taxation is

The Budget-Mr. Fisher concerned they cannot afford to assume heavier burdens with regard to silviculture, particularly relatively expensive regeneration measures. They take the position that they cannot do this until the tax position has been cleared up by the only people who are able to do it, the federal government. And until this is done, then for just so long will they be able to use this as an excuse, if it is an excuse.
So from this point of view, in particular, I am disappointed that the minister did not announce measures which the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources (Mr. Hamilton) indicated he intended to carry out, namely arrangements for a study of the taxation position of this very important industry.
As far as this point is concerned, it seems to me that the whole future of our forests is not so much in jeopardy as that it has reached a turning point. I think there is a growing sensitivity on the part of these very large organizations about their responsibilities, and it seems to me also that many professional foresters, the people who have some indication as to where we should go, feel that if we could just get over this particular argument we might get somewhere. That is why I voice this somewhat out of the way disappointment with this budget.
